questions.title: How does the Second Circuit analyze the 'purpose and character' factor in a fair‑use defense when the infringer’s intent conflicts with a reasonable observer’s perception?
questions.question_body: In this opinion, the court held that the videos were “transformative” because a reasonable observer would view them as conveying hope, strength, etc., not merely as money‑making content. I’m unsure how the court balances the parties’ subjective intent against the objective observer standard. What case law underpins this shift, and how is it applied at the pleading stage?

questions.title: Why does the court conclude that the ‘bad‑faith’ representations made by Kimmel do not invalidate the fair‑use defense?
questions.question_body: Santos cited Harper & Row to argue that Kimmel’s false representations demonstrate bad faith, which should negate fair use. The court says the Supreme Court has since moved away from that assertion. Which cases establish that the privity‑or‑bad‑faith requirement is no longer a part of the fair‑use analysis, and how does the court apply them to this case?

questions.title: On what grounds are Santos’s breach‑of‑contract claims deemed preempted by the Copyright Act?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed Santos’s first two state‑law claims claiming they were preempted by the Copyright Act. The appellate court says it does not need to resolve the issue because the claims fail to state a claim. Yet I’m unsure which preemption doctrine—section 202(a) or 302(a)—is at issue and why the court treats it as essentially a deferral. Could someone explain the preemption analysis that applies to contract claims arising from alleged copyright infringement?

questions.title: What statutory authority does the court rely on to deem Santos’s breach of contract claim under the Cameo Terms of Service unenforceable as a non‑party?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites a strong Illinois presumption against conferring benefits to non‑contracting third parties. How does this presumption interact with the specific language in the Cameo Terms of Service, and are there any alternative theories (e.g., third‑party beneficiary doctrine or implied‑in‑fact contract) that Santos could have plausibly relied on?

questions.title: Why does the court allow judicial notice of the copyright registrations in the factual matrix?
questions.question_body: The court says it may take judicial notice of ‘copyright registrations[] as published in the Copyright Office’s registry.’ I’m unclear about when a court can elect to take judicial notice of copyright registrations and how that affects the fair‑use analysis.

questions.title: Under what conditions does a plaintiff have to plead an ‘actual out‑of‑pocket loss’ for a fraudulent inducement claim in New York?
questions.question_body: Santos’s fraudulent inducement claim was dismissed for failure to allege an out‑of‑pocket loss. I’d like a clearer sense of the New York standard for out‑of‑pocket loss in fraud claims and how a plaintiff can plead it effectively.

questions.title: Does fair use analysis at the pleading stage address the fourth fair‑use factor (market effect) if the alleged infringing work is not a direct substitute for the original?
questions.question_body: The court notes that Santos has not suffered market harm because the videos were “published on the same day they were created.” How does the court's reasoning address the market‑effect factor when the alleged use is purely transformative and not a market substitute?

questions.title: What evidentiary standard does the Second Circuit apply when determining whether a fair‑use claim can be dismissed at the Rule 12(b)(6) level?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites TCA Television Corp. as allowing dismissal when fair use is ‘so clearly established by a complaint.’ What specific pleading standards or evidence do courts look for before dismissing a claim on fair‑use grounds?
